doc.title: James Chirillo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 12, 2007

title: Arriving at North Texas State as a self-taught rock guitarist
summary: At 22 Chirillo was self-taught, had not heard Charlie Parker, and got into North Texas in 1975 on community college grades with a Mundell Lowe guitar scholarship.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: When you were at North Texas State, I’m going to jump around a little bit, but I’ve got that on my mind. How much of the — I don’t know if you can give me a percentage — but how much of what you learned there turned out to be useful in the real world of a gigging, working musician?

Well in that I was basically about one step removed from a blank slate when I went down there, you know as a self-taught rock & roll guitar player, so I had just started to get into different jazz guitar players when I went down there. Joe Pass and Grant Green, guys like that, of course Wes. But I hadn’t even heard of Charlie Parker when I went down there, and I was, when was that, so I was 22.
Yeah. I was into King Crimson and those kind of guys.

Yeah, right. Robert Fripp, those guys. I mean of course and Hendrix and all those, Jimmy Page, you name it. So when I went down there, anything that I got exposed to was great. And they had a great classical department too, let alone the jazz department.
What did you get accepted as, and what got you in there? Your compositions?

No. It’s not like, I mean back then, and we’re talking ’75, it was a state university, I mean it still is for that matter. But it wasn’t — the whole financial outlay was much less. I remember even then a semester was something between eight and twelve hundred bucks, for a semester’s worth of classes. A full load. And roughly the dorm was probably about the same. And after my first year there I ended up getting like a guitar scholarship that Mundell Lowe was paying for, it was like a hundred bucks a semester but if you won a scholarship like that then it enabled you to get in-state rates. So that basically, that hundred dollars took care of the semester’s tuition at the in-state rate. So it made my dad happy. But still, I mean that’s the thing. So I mean I’m not really sure — I’d gone to — my grades weren’t that great in high school because I was young and savage, but when I decided — I took a year off from high school before I got into college and I took two years or so at Bellevue Community College, where I figured I would take all the required kind of things. So I took math and history or this and that. And of course it was — you
know if I decide to use my brain it’s going to come out okay, so in high school I wasn’t using my brain so much but what the heck.
You were using your King Crimson.

When you’re that age — oh Lord, no. I’m not even going to go where I was just thinking. Stupidity knows no bounds. But that’s beside the point. Suffice it to say I got, you know, like a 3.9 or whatever the heck it was when I was going to the community college, so I sent those transcripts down and that’s probably why they accepted me. You know ‘cause musically I was pretty savage.
